html:
The script used to write Meroitic, the language of the kingdom of Kush, from about the 3rd century BCE to the 4th century CE. Scholars can read its sounds but still understand only a little of the language.

Before this time, the kings of Kush wrote in Egyptian. When the capital moved to Meroë, scribes created a way to write their own tongue. It came in two forms. A cursive one, used for most texts, grew from Egyptian Demotic writing. A formal one, used on royal monuments, borrowed signs from Egyptian hieroglyphs. Both had only 23 signs, used mostly as letters.

In 1909 the British scholar Francis Llewellyn Griffith worked out the sound values from names that appear in both Egyptian and Meroitic. But Meroitic has no close living relative, and no long bilingual text has been found, so most words remain a mystery.

It is one of the oldest written languages of Africa after Egyptian. Writing in the region later passed to Greek, Coptic and Old Nubian in the kingdoms of Christian Nubia.
